title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the gods' search for what could carry the high chant. Nose, speech, eye, ear and mind all went both ways. The main breath held. Did you come back to it? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la. Plenty of songs on the radio have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. They aren't in the dictionary. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, all together, louder than the verses. A syllable with no meaning can carry a whole stadium. Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped in between the words of the verse, there to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't. Today: the sounds between the words.
screen: `NA NA NA. HEY HEY.` → `NOT IN ANY DICTIONARY.` → `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat. And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are called stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does. They're there for the song. Then the Chandogya turns to them, and it gives the stobhas the world. In paraphrase, it says: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha. And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food. Hold on to that. The sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song. Earth, wind, moon, all riding in a syllable that has no dictionary meaning. Readers of the text take this in more than one way. Some hear it as a meditation, a way for the singer to hold the whole world in mind while chanting. Some hear a deeper point about sound itself: that meaning isn't only in what a word says, it's in what a sound can hold. The Chandogya doesn't settle that for us. It just refuses to throw the small sounds away. On an ordinary day, there are stobhas everywhere. The hmm when a friend is talking. The oh when someone hands you coffee. The sigh at the end of a long day. Nothing in a dictionary. Not nothing.
screen: `STRETCHED, REPEATED, FILLED IN.` · `STOBHAS: HAU, HAI, AUHOYI.` · `THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.` · `THE SMALL SOUNDS ARE NOT THROWN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a small sound your full attention. Sit, and breathe in. On the out-breath, let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears. Let it be just a sound, no meaning. Breathe in again. On the next out-breath, make the same sound, and this time let it hold one thing: the ground under you, or the air in the room. Keep going, one breath, one sound, one thing it carries. If silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, you can let it be prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Sama Veda as song. In the chant, small sounds called stobhas carry the melody, and the Chandogya pairs them with the world. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Today, listen for the sounds between words, the hmm, the oh, the sigh. Treat one as if it carries something. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: In Sama Veda chanting, the words of a verse are stretched and repeated and joined by syllables called stobhas, and the chants are learned from a teacher by ear.

fork.setup: you're reading the chant for meaning, and you hit hau, hai, auhoyi. they aren't words. what do you do?
options: pair them with the world, as the Chandogya does
fork.reveal: the Chandogya pairs them with the world: this world is hau, the wind is hai, the moon is atha.

original.note: Sanskrit: a syllable added in Sama Veda chant, outside the words of the verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: the odd syllables in a chant are filler.
what it means: the Chandogya pairs those syllables with the world: earth, wind, moon.
what a scholar hears: stobha, the non-lexical chant syllables of the sāmans; Chandogya 1.13 lists them with their correspondences (hāu, this world; hāi, the wind; atha, the moon).
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
